lines.text: Black mountains above the Adriatic, a land of prince-bishops that kept its freedom, then a kingdom, Yugoslavia and independence. This is the story of Montenegro.
In the ninth century, a Slavic state called Duklja held the coast and the mountains, the first of the Montenegrin lands.
In 1482 Cetinje was founded high in the mountains. It became the old royal capital.
From Cetinje the prince-bishops kept the Ottomans out. One of them, Petar the Second Njegos, was also a poet, and wrote The Mountain Wreath.
Nicholas, born in 1841, would rule for more than half a century, and in 1910 make himself king.
In 1852 the prince-bishops gave way to princes, and Montenegro became a principality, recognised by the great powers in 1878.
Milo Djukanovic, born in 1962, would serve as prime minister or president for most of three decades.
Jakov Milatovic, born in 1986, would defeat him and become president in 2023.
After joining Yugoslavia in 1918, Montenegro stayed with Serbia when it broke up, in a loose union that kept the name Yugoslavia.
In 2006 Montenegro held a referendum, and its people voted to leave the union and stand alone.
And in 2017 the small mountain country joined NATO, tying its future to the West.
From the prince-bishops of Cetinje to a free nation on the Adriatic, Montenegro's story continues.
